Apple___Apple_scab.impact: Can significantly reduce fruit quality and yield. Severe infections may cause defoliation. Infected fruit is unmarketable and reduces commercial value.

Apple___Black_rot.spread: Spreads through rain-splash from infected fruit and cankers. Spores infect through wounds and natural openings. Can persist in dead wood and infected fruit.
Apple___Black_rot.impact: Reduces fruit quality and marketability. Can cause branch dieback and tree decline if cankers girdled branches. Stored fruit can continue to rot after harvest.

Tomato___Early_blight.symptoms: Brown circular lesions with concentric rings (target-spot appearance) on lower leaves first. Dark brown spots on stems and petioles form. Leaves gradually yellow and drop. Fruit develops brown spots.
Tomato___Early_blight.spread: Spreads via airborne spores. Requires 2-5 days of leaf wetness and moderate temperatures (60-75°F). More severe with overhead irrigation and poor air circulation.
Tomato___Early_blight.impact: Defoliates plants and reduces yield. Infected fruit is unmarketable. Can cause 10-30% yield loss if untreated. Storage rot may occur.
prevention: Remove infected leaves and lower foliage to avoid soil splash
Use drip irrigation, never overhead water
Space plants properly for air circulation
Practice crop rotation (3+ years without tomatoes)
Use disease-resistant varieties
Remove plant debris from field after harvest
treatment: Apply fungicides (mancozeb, chlorothalonil, azoxystrobin) starting when disease appears
Spray at 7-10 day intervals or more frequently if wet conditions persist
Remove heavily infected leaves and lower foliage
Continue fungicide applications until end of season
Ensure thorough spray coverage of all remaining foliage

Tomato___healthy.cause: No disease detected. Plant shows normal growth with no signs of infection.
Tomato___healthy.symptoms: No disease symptoms visible. Leaves are green with normal morphology. Stems are healthy. Fruit is developing normally without blemishes.
Tomato___healthy.impact: Healthy tomato plant with good fruit production potential. Continue regular monitoring and best management practices.
prevention: Monitor regularly for disease and pest detection
Maintain consistent watering and nutrition
Use drip irrigation to keep foliage dry
Provide proper support and pruning
Scout for insect pests that may vector disease
Apply preventive fungicides if disease pressure is high in region
treatment: No treatment required
Continue regular care and monitoring
Watch for any emerging symptoms

Tomato___Late_blight.cause: Oomycete (water mold) infection caused by Phytophthora infestans. Requires cool, wet conditions to develop and spread rapidly. Can devastate tomato crops in conducive weather.
Tomato___Late_blight.symptoms: Water-soaked, dark lesions on leaves and stems. White fungal growth appears on undersides of lesions in humid conditions. Entire plants can collapse quickly. Fruit develops water-soaked, irregular lesions.
Tomato___Late_blight.spread: Spreads via airborne zoospores when leaves stay wet and temperatures are cool (below 65°F). Can spread hundreds of miles via wind and spores.
Tomato___Late_blight.impact: Can destroy tomato plants rapidly in cool, wet conditions. Causes significant fruit rot and loss. Most serious tomato disease in cool-season climates.
prevention: Avoid overhead watering; use drip irrigation only
Space plants properly for air circulation
Start fungicide sprays early in the season, especially if weather is cool and wet
Spray every 7-10 days during high-risk periods
Remove volunteer tomato plants near new plantings
Use resistant varieties if available
treatment: Apply chlorothalonil, mancozeb, or copper-based fungicides immediately when disease is suspected
Spray preventively before wet period if possible
Remove infected plants completely to prevent spread
Apply fungicides every 5-7 days in wet conditions
Ensure thorough coverage of all leaves and stems

Tomato___Leaf_Mold.cause: Fungal infection caused by Fulvia fulva. Thrives in warm, humid conditions inside greenhouses. Survives on infected plant debris and in soil.
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.symptoms: Yellow spots on upper leaf surface with olive-green to gray fuzzy fungal growth on undersides. Lesions start on lower leaves and progress upward. Leaves may wither and drop but fruit is not directly infected.
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.spread: Spreads via airborne spores. Requires high humidity (> 85%) and warm temperatures (70-75°F). More common in greenhouses where humidity is high.
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.impact: Causes defoliation which reduces photosynthesis and fruit development. Can reduce yield significantly in greenhouse conditions. Less common in open-field tomatoes.
prevention: Improve air circulation and ventilation in greenhouses
Space plants properly and avoid overcrowding
Use drip irrigation—never wet foliage
Reduce humidity through ventilation and dehumidifiers
Remove lower leaves as plants grow
Disinfect greenhouse structures and tools
treatment: Apply chlorothalonil, mancozeb, or sulfur fungicides every 7-10 days
Remove lower infected leaves to reduce spore source
Improve greenhouse ventilation to reduce humidity
Apply fungicides early before infection becomes severe
Continue treatments throughout growing season in high-humidity conditions

Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.cause: Fungal infection caused by Septoria lycopersici. Fungus survives in infected plant debris and seeds. Spreads during wet conditions.
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.symptoms: Small, circular lesions with dark borders and gray centers on leaves. Black dots (spore-producing structures) visible in lesion centers. Lesions start on lower leaves and progress upward. Heavy infection causes defoliation.
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.spread: Spreads via airborne spores and water-splash. Requires wet conditions for spore release and infection. More severe in fields with overhead irrigation.
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.impact: Causes progressive defoliation from lower to upper leaves. Reduces photosynthesis and fruit quality. Can cause up to 30% yield loss if untreated.
prevention: Use disease-free seeds from certified sources
Remove infected plant debris after harvest
Avoid overhead watering; use drip irrigation
Space plants properly for air circulation
Remove lower leaves as plants grow
Practice crop rotation (2-year minimum)
treatment: Apply chlorothalonil or mancozeb fungicides at early disease signs
Spray at 7-10 day intervals if wet conditions persist
Remove heavily infected leaves, starting with lower foliage
Improve air circulation through pruning
Continue fungicide applications until fruit reaches mature green stage

Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.cause: Pest infestation by spider mites (Tetranychus urticae). Not a fungal or bacterial disease but a arachnid pest. Populations explode in hot, dry conditions.
Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.symptoms: Fine stippling or yellowing on leaves from mites piercing cells to feed. Fine webbing on leaf undersides and between leaflets. Leaves become bronze and wither. Heavy infestations can cause entire plants to drop leaves.
Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.spread: Spreads by wind-blown mites moving between plants. Populations build rapidly in warm, dry conditions. Can spread through irrigation water.
Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.impact: Heavy infestation reduces photosynthesis, weakens plants, and reduces yield and fruit quality. Can cause complete plant death in severe cases.
prevention: Maintain adequate humidity and avoid drought stress
Use drip irrigation rather than overhead watering
Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization
Monitor plants regularly for early mite presence
Release beneficial insects like ladybugs and predatory mites
Spray with water to remove mites and webbing
treatment: Apply miticide when spider mites are detected (sulfur, abamectin, or bifenthrin)
Spray undersides of leaves thoroughly for good coverage
Use neem oil or horticultural oil insecticides
Alternate miticide products to prevent resistance
Repeat applications at 7-10 day intervals if mites persist

Tomato___Target_Spot.cause: Fungal infection caused by Corynespora cassiicola. Survives in plant debris and infected seeds. Develops in warm, humid conditions.
Tomato___Target_Spot.symptoms: Circular brown lesions with concentric rings resembling a target. Lesions typically appear on lower leaves first. Yellow halo may surround lesions. Heavy infection causes defoliation.
Tomato___Target_Spot.spread: Spreads via airborne spores and water-splash. Requires moisture and warm temperatures (70-80°F) for infection. More severe in humid, wet conditions.
Tomato___Target_Spot.impact: Causes defoliation and reduces photosynthesis. Weakens plant vigor and reduces yield. Can cause significant crop loss in warm, humid regions.
prevention: Use disease-free seed from certified sources
Avoid overhead irrigation; use drip irrigation
Space plants properly for air circulation
Remove lower leaves to prevent spore contact
Remove infected plant debris after harvest
Practice crop rotation with non-solanaceous crops
treatment: Apply fungicides (chlorothalonil, mancozeb, azoxystrobin) at early disease signs
Spray at 7-10 day intervals if conditions favor disease
Remove heavily infected leaves and lower foliage
Improve air circulation through pruning
Continue fungicide applications throughout growing season

Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.cause: Viral infection caused by Tomato Mosaic Virus. Transmitted through plant sap contact and contaminated tools. Survives in infected seeds and plant debris.
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.symptoms: Mosaic pattern of light and dark green on leaves. Leaves may be distorted or crinkled with yellowing between veins. Fruit may show yellow and red blotches. Plants may be stunted.
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.spread: Spreads via contact with infected plant sap through leaves, hands, and tools. Pruning infected plants spreads virus. Can survive in soil on tobacco residue.
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.impact: Reduces yield and fruit quality. Stunted plants produce smaller fruit. No cure once infected. Can persist in crop residue.
prevention: Use disease-resistant varieties (ToMV resistance is often indicated as 'V' in variety name)
Do not smoke or allow tobacco use in greenhouse/field
Divide work crew into tobacco users and non-users
Disinfect tools with 10% bleach between plants
Remove infected plants immediately to prevent spread
Use disease-free seed from certified sources
treatment: Remove infected plants completely to prevent spread—there is no chemical cure
Disinfect tools and equipment with 10% bleach or Lysol
Wash hands and change clothes after handling infected plants
Do not allow tobacco use in growing areas
Plant resistant varieties for future crops

Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.cause: Viral infection caused by Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus. Transmitted exclusively by whiteflies (Bemisia tabaci). Cannot move through plant sap.
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.symptoms: Yellowing and curling of leaf margins. Leaves become smaller and distorted. Yellow spotting may appear. Plants are severely stunted. Fruit production stops.
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.spread: Spread ONLY by whiteflies, especially the B biotype (Mediterranean race). Cannot be transmitted by contact or pruning. Whiteflies acquire virus and transmit to new plants.
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.impact: Causes severe stunting and loss of fruit production. Infected plants become unproductive. Causes significant crop loss in whitefly-prone regions.
prevention: Control whitefly populations with insecticides, parasitic wasps, or reflective mulches
Use virus-resistant varieties when available
Monitor for early symptoms and remove infected plants
Use yellow sticky traps to monitor and control whiteflies
Control broadleaf weeds that host whiteflies
Avoid bringing infected plants from other sources
treatment: Remove infected plants immediately—no cure for systemic infection
Control whitefly populations aggressively using insecticides or biological controls
Use reflective mulches to repel whiteflies
Monitor plants closely for early symptom detection
Plant resistant varieties for future seasons
